name: NetworkPolicy: control egress
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Drill EVERY NetworkPolicy corner harder than the exam: default-deny ingress & egress, allow-by-pod-label, allow-by-namespace, the AND-vs-OR peer trap, port+protocol scoping, ipBlock with except, allow-DNS, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on the policy spec, per requirement. (kindnet does not enforce policies, so grading is on the authored spec.)

questions.title: Default-deny egress + allow DNS
questions.teach:
Egress isolation mirrors ingress: empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, and only the egress rules you need. Blocking all egress breaks **DNS**, so you allow port 53 to `kube-system` (CoreDNS) via a `to` `namespaceSelector` plus `ports`.

**Gotcha:** CoreDNS answers on port 53 over **both UDP and TCP** — list both; UDP alone fails on large responses.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `default-deny-egress-allow-dns` that selects **all** pods, is egress-isolated, and allows egress **only** to port 53 (UDP and TCP) of `kube-system`.

Target: empty `podSelector`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, one egress rule with a `to` `namespaceSelector` matching `kube-system` and `ports` UDP/53 and TCP/53.
questions.hint: `podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Egress]`, then `egress: [{ to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } } }], ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53},{protocol: TCP, port: 53}] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress-allow-dns
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
EOF

verification.description: default-deny-egress-allow-dns: empty podSelector, Egress, DNS UDP+TCP/53 to kube-system

questions.eli5:
So far we've been controlling who comes **in** (ingress). Egress is the mirror image: controlling where your pods are allowed to reach **out** to.

A **default-deny egress** policy is like putting every pod under house arrest for outgoing calls: select all pods (`podSelector: {}`), say "I'm governing outbound" (`policyTypes: [Egress]`), and allow only the destinations you list.

But here's the catch almost everyone trips on the first time. The moment you block all outbound, your pods can't do **DNS** anymore. Before a pod can talk to `my-service`, it has to ask the cluster's phone book — **CoreDNS** — "what's the IP for that name?" If you've blocked everything outbound, that phone-book lookup fails, and *every* connection dies before it even starts, with confusing "name resolution" errors.

So a safe default-deny egress almost always pairs with an **allow-DNS** rule: let pods reach **port 53** in the `kube-system` namespace (where CoreDNS lives).

**Watch out for:**

- **Blocking egress breaks DNS.** Without an allow-53 rule, name lookups fail and nothing connects. This is *the* classic egress gotcha.
- **CoreDNS answers on port 53 over BOTH UDP and TCP.** List both. UDP handles most queries, but large responses fall back to TCP — UDP-only silently fails on those.
- **DNS lives in `kube-system`.** Target it with a `to` `namespaceSelector` matching `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system`.
- **`policyTypes: [Egress]` must be set** — without it (and with no egress block), nothing is governed.
- **Egress only.** Ingress is untouched by this policy.
- **Additive & CNI-dependent.** This sets the outbound floor; other allow-rules add more destinations. Needs a policy-enforcing CNI (kindnet won't actually block).
questions.deepDive:
## Default-deny egress + allow DNS — full rundown

### Mental model
Egress is the mirror of ingress: selecting a pod for the **Egress** direction flips it to **default-deny outbound**, and each `egress` rule adds back a permitted destination. The catch unique to egress: blocking everything also blocks **DNS**, so almost every default-deny-egress must be paired with an allow-DNS rule to remain usable.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress-allow-dns
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}            # all pods in the namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system   # CoreDNS lives here
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
```

### Why DNS breaks — the mechanism
1. App calls `connect("db.netpol-learn.svc.cluster.local")`.
2. The pod first sends a **DNS query to CoreDNS** (ClusterIP in `kube-system`) on **port 53**.
3. With default-deny egress and no DNS allow, that query is dropped.
4. Resolution times out → the app never even gets an IP → **every** outbound connection fails with name-resolution errors, which look unrelated to NetworkPolicy.

### Why BOTH UDP and TCP on 53
| Protocol | Role |
|---|---|
| **UDP/53** | Default transport for almost all DNS queries |
| **TCP/53** | Fallback for responses > 512 bytes (truncated UDP), zone transfers, large records |

UDP-only works until a response is large (many A records, DNSSEC, etc.), then silently fails. Always allow **both**.

### Ingress vs egress symmetry
| | Ingress | Egress |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | inbound to selected pods | outbound from selected pods |
| Peer key | `from` | `to` |
| policyTypes | `Ingress` | `Egress` |
| Default-deny | select + no `ingress` rules | select + no `egress` rules |
| DNS concern | none | **must allow 53** |

### Hardening the DNS rule further
To allow DNS to *only* the CoreDNS pods (not every pod in kube-system), AND the namespace with a pod selector:
```yaml
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
    podSelector:       { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }   # CoreDNS label
  ports:
  - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
```
(`k8s-app: kube-dns` is the standard CoreDNS pod label.)

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol default-deny-egress-allow-dns -o yaml
kubectl get ns kube-system --show-labels
# from a test pod, confirm resolution works after applying:
kubectl -n netpol-learn run t --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it -- nslookup kubernetes.default
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Forgetting the DNS allow** is the #1 egress mistake — everything "mysteriously" fails to connect.
- **UDP-only DNS** passes small lookups but breaks on large responses — list **TCP/53 too**.
- **`policyTypes: [Egress]` is required**; without it (and no egress block) nothing is governed.
- **`to` peers and `from` peers follow the same AND/OR rules** — separate list items OR, selectors in one entry AND.
- **Egress only** — this policy does not touch inbound.
- **Additive** — it sets the outbound floor; other policies can only add destinations.
- **CNI enforcement required**; kindnet stores but does not enforce — grading is on the authored spec.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
    ports:
    - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
    - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
```

questions.title: Restrict egress to a specific pod and port
questions.teach:
For least privilege, pin egress to the exact destination a workload needs: a `to` `podSelector` matching the target pods plus the exact `ports`. A `to` `podSelector` alone matches destination pods **in the policy's own namespace**.

**Gotcha:** this policy covers only the DB hop — the pod still needs the separate DNS allow (port 53) or name resolution breaks before it reaches the destination.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-egress-to-db` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows egress **only** to pods labelled `app=db` on **TCP port 5432**.

Target: `podSelector` app=web; `policyTypes: [Egress]`; one egress rule with a `to` `podSelector` matching `app=db` and `ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]`.
questions.hint: `podSelector.matchLabels.app: web`, `egress: [{ to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } } }], ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-to-db
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: db
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
EOF

verification.description: allow-egress-to-db: app=web → podSelector app=db on TCP/5432

questions.eli5:
Least privilege means a pod should only be able to reach the **exact** thing it needs — nothing more. Here, your `app=web` pods need to talk to the database (`app=db`) on its one port (5432), and nowhere else.

Think of it like giving a courier a single pre-addressed envelope: *"you may deliver only to the database's door, number 5432, and no other building or door exists for you."* An **egress `to` podSelector** names that destination by its label (`app=db`), and **`ports`** pins it to the one door (TCP 5432).

One detail to remember: a `to` `podSelector` on its own only sees destination pods in the **same namespace** as the policy — just like the ingress side. If the database lived in another namespace, you'd also need a `namespaceSelector`.

**Watch out for:**

- **This covers only the database hop.** The web pod *still* needs a separate DNS allow (port 53 to kube-system) — otherwise it can't even look up the database's name, and the connection dies before it starts. Egress policies stack: one for DNS, one for the DB.
- **A `to` `podSelector` is namespace-local.** Reaching a DB in another namespace needs a `namespaceSelector` added in the same peer entry (AND).
- **`ports` scopes it to 5432.** Without `ports`, the pod could reach `app=db` on *any* port; with it, only TCP 5432.
- **Labels must match exactly** — `app=db` ≠ `app=DB`.
- **Additive & CNI-dependent.** Selecting `app=web` for egress flips it to default-deny outbound; this only re-opens the DB path. Needs a policy-enforcing CNI (kindnet won't actually block).
questions.deepDive:
## Restrict egress to a specific pod and port — full rundown

### Mental model
This is least-privilege egress: after the Egress default-deny flip, you add back exactly **one** permitted destination — the DB pods (`app=db`) on their one port (TCP 5432). A `to` **`podSelector`** names destination pods by label (own namespace by default); **`ports`** pins the protocol/port. Everything else outbound stays denied.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-to-db
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web                 # pods this governs (sources)
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: db              # allowed destination (same ns)
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
```

### Fields at a glance
| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `spec.podSelector` | `app=web` | which pods' outbound this governs |
| `egress[].to[].podSelector` | `app=db` | allowed destination pods (own ns) |
| `egress[].ports` | TCP/5432 | only this port/protocol to those pods |

### Namespace scope — same rule as ingress
A `to` `podSelector` **alone** only matches destination pods in the **policy's own namespace**. For a DB in another namespace, AND a namespaceSelector into the same peer entry:
```yaml
to:
- namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: data } }
  podSelector:       { matchLabels: { app: db } }
```

### DNS is a SEPARATE requirement
This policy permits the DB hop **only**. Because selecting `app=web` for Egress flips it to default-deny outbound, the pod also loses DNS. The app resolves `db...svc` via CoreDNS **before** it can reach 5432, so you need the DNS allow too. NetworkPolicies are additive, so apply both — they combine:
```yaml
egress:
- to:                                 # DNS
  - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
  ports:
  - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
- to:                                 # DB
  - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } }
  ports:
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
```
(Either two rules in one policy as above, or two separate policies — same result.)

### Ingress-side matters too
Egress on the web pod lets it *send* to the DB. For packets to actually flow, the **DB pod's ingress** must also permit `app=web` on 5432 if the DB namespace has a default-deny-ingress. NetworkPolicy is evaluated **independently at both ends**.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-egress-to-db -o yaml
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-egress-to-db \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.egress[0]}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Forgetting DNS** — the DB connection dies at name resolution, not at 5432. Add the DNS allow.
- **`to` podSelector is namespace-local** — cross-namespace DB needs a namespaceSelector (AND, same entry).
- **No `ports`** → all ports to `app=db` allowed; add `ports` to scope to 5432.
- **Both ends enforce independently** — the DB's ingress policy must also allow `app=web`.
- **Label typos silently block** (`app=db` ≠ `app=DB`).
- **Additive** — only reopens the DB path; all other egress stays denied by the flip.
- **CNI enforcement required**; kindnet does not enforce — grading is on the spec.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } }
    ports:
    - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
  # plus a DNS allow (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system)
```
